CHAPTER XCVII

A priest is never more thoroughly a priest than in the chamber of death,
Gerard did the last offices of the Church for the departed, just as
he should have done them for his smallest parishioner. He did this
mechanically, then sat down stupefied by the sudden and tremendous blow,
and not yet realizing the pangs of bereavement. Then in a transport of
religious enthusiasm he kneeled and thanked Heaven for her Christian
end.

And then all his thought was to take her away from strangers, and lay
her in his own churchyard. That very evening a covered cart with one
horse started for Gouda, and in it was a coffin, and a broken-hearted
man lying with his arms and chin resting on it.

The mourner's short-lived energy had exhausted itself in the necessary
preparations, and now he lay crushed, clinging to the cold lead that
held her.

The man of whom the cart was hired walked by the horse's head and did
not speak to him, and when he baited the horse spoke but in a whisper
respecting that mute agony. But when he stopped for the night, he and
the landlord made a well-meaning attempt to get the mourner away to take
some rest and food. But Gerard repulsed them, and when they persisted,
almost snarled at them, like a faithful dog, and clung to the cold lead
all night. So then they drew a cloak over him, and left him in peace.

And at noon the sorrowful cart came up to the manse, and there were
full a score of parishioners collected with one little paltry trouble or
another. They had missed the parson already. And when they saw what it
was, and saw their healer so stricken down, they raised a loud wail of
grief, and it roused him from his lethargy of woe, and he saw where he
was, and their faces, and tried to speak to them, “Oh, my children! my
children!” he cried; but choked with anguish, could say no more.

Yet the next day, spite of all remonstrances, he buried her himself,
and read the service with a voice that only trembled now and then, Many
tears fell upon her grave. And when the service ended he stayed there
standing like a statue, and the people left the churchyard out of
respect.

He stood like one in a dream till the sexton, who was, as most men are,
a fool, began to fill in the grave without giving him due warning.

But at the sound of earth falling on her Gerard uttered a piercing
scream.

The sexton forbore.

Gerard staggered and put his hand to his breast. The sexton supported
him, and called for help.

Jorian Ketel, who lingered near mourning his benefactress, ran into the
churchyard, and the two supported Gerard into the manse.

“Ah, Jorian! good Jorian!” said he, “something snapped within me; I
felt it, and I heard it; here, Jorian, here;” and he put his hand to his
breast.

A priest is never so wholly priest as when the room is darkened, the candles burn low, and Death—patient, noiseless, and absolute—sits at the bedside like an old acquaintance. Gerard did the last offices as the Church had taught him, word following word, sign following sign, as steadily as he had done for the poorest hind that ever lay with clay on his boots. His hands moved; his voice obeyed; the rites went on with a terrible propriety, as if order itself could keep calamity at bay.

When all was finished, he sat down, stunned, his mind refusing the shape of what had happened. Grief had not yet found its teeth. The chamber had its own small sounds—the faint wick-sputter, the soft settling of linen, the far-off creak of timber in the house—each sound too clear, too near, because her breathing was no longer there to round them and make them homely.

Then, as though a spring within him leaped, he fell upon his knees and, in a sudden blaze of religious fervour, thanked Heaven—not for the stroke, but for her Christian end; for the seal of peace upon her; for the prayers said in time; for the merciful ordering of her last hour. He clung to that, because it was something he could name. And after that one fierce act of praise, thought narrowed to a single, burning duty: to take her away from strangers and lay her in his own earth, among the graves that knew his footstep and the psalms of his voice.

That very evening a covered cart, with one horse, set out for Gouda. In it lay a coffin; and beside it—so close that his breath seemed meant to warm the metal—lay a broken-hearted man with his arms and chin resting on the lead that held her. The haste and labour of making ready—ordering boards, seeing to the fitting, the decent covering, the necessary papers and words to men who did not understand—had spent the little force his soul could muster. Now he lay crushed, as if the cart-wheels ran over his very heart, and clung to the cold lid like a man clinging to a plank in black water.

The carter walked by the horse’s head and did not speak to him. There was a kind of reverence in his silence, as there is in a kitchen when a great pot has boiled over and scalded some one—no loud calls, no clatter, only the careful hush that says: pain is here, tread softly. When he baited the horse at a wayside, he spoke even then but in a whisper, out of respect to that dumb agony that lay inside the tilt. The world outside went on with its ordinary noises—wind in the hedges, a distant dog, the far ring of a smith’s hammer on iron—yet those sounds were muffled by the cart’s canvas and by Gerard’s own inward roar.

At the night stop the carter and the landlord made a well-meant attempt to coax him down, to get him into a room, to put food before him and make him sleep. The smell of bread and broth came to the doorway—honest, saving smells that had comforted men a thousand times—yet to him they were like a language he could not speak. He repulsed them; and when they persisted, he almost snarled, not as a priest, not as a reasoning man, but like a faithful dog guarding what has been given him to guard. He clung to the lead all night, refusing even the little mercy of a pillow, as if to move an inch away were to betray her.

So they drew a cloak over him and left him in peace.

At noon next day the sorrowful cart came up to the manse. There were full a score of parishioners gathered there already, each with his own poor grievance—a cow gone lame, a child feverish, a neighbour’s boundary disputed, a husband too fond of the alehouse. They had missed the parson and came, as folk do, for counsel and for comfort. But when they saw what the cart bore, and saw their healer stricken down like any other man, the crowd’s small murmurs broke into a loud wail of grief.

That human cry, rising all at once like a gust through trees, startled him from his lethargy. He lifted his head, and the familiar faces swam before him—faces he had known in sowing-time and harvest, in christening and confession. He tried to speak; and the words that came were not sermon, not rebuke, not doctrine, but sheer fatherhood. “Oh, my children! my children!” he cried. Then anguish closed his throat, and he could say no more.

Yet the next day, in spite of all remonstrance, he buried her himself. He would not be spared that final service, as if any other hand at the grave were an intrusion. He read the appointed words, and his voice only trembled now and then, like a bell that has a crack yet still gives a true note. Many tears fell upon the earth that received her—tears of women who had come to her for kindness, of men who had respected her, of children who had felt her hand upon their hair; and tears, too, of those who did not know her well but knew what it is for a household’s heart to be taken away.

When the service ended, Gerard stayed there in the churchyard, standing like a statue. The people withdrew, one by one, out of respect, leaving him alone with the new mound and the raw smell of turned soil—a smell that in other seasons meant potatoes planted, cabbages set, the promise of stew in winter; but now meant only that the ground had swallowed his life’s companion. The birds went on with their thin notes in the yews; somewhere beyond the wall a cart rumbled; the village breathed. He stood as one in a dream, hearing everything and understanding nothing.

The sexton, who was—as most men are—a fool, began to fill in the grave without giving due warning. The first patter of earth upon the coffin-lid came sharp and sudden, like hail on a roof. At that sound Gerard uttered a piercing scream, so wild that it made the very air shudder.

The sexton stopped short. Gerard staggered, and his hand flew to his breast as if something within had given way like a snapped cord. The sexton caught him, clumsy but frightened into gentleness, and called for help. Jorian Ketel, who had lingered near, mourning his benefactress, ran into the churchyard at once; and between them they supported Gerard to the manse.

“Ah, Jorian! good Jorian!” Gerard gasped, with a dreadful simplicity. “Something snapped within me; I felt it, and I heard it; here, Jorian, here;” and he pressed his hand hard upon his breast, as if to keep the broken place from widening.
